title: Bonaventure
wiki_lead:
Bonaventure (born Giovanni di Fidanza; 1221 – 15 July 1274) was an Italian Catholic Franciscan bishop, cardinal, scholastic theologian and philosopher.
The seventh Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor, he also served for a time as Bishop of Albano. He was canonised on 14 April 1482 by Pope Sixtus IV. In 1588 Pope Sixtus V declared him a Doctor of the Church named as the "Seraphic Doctor" (Latin: Doctor Seraphicus). His feast day is 15 July.
Many writings from the Middle Ages once attributed to him have been subsequently re-classified under the name "Pseudo-Bonaventure".
wiki_excerpt:
Bonaventure (born Giovanni di Fidanza; 1221 – 15 July 1274) was an Italian Catholic Franciscan bishop, cardinal, scholastic theologian and philosopher.
The seventh Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor, he also served for a time as Bishop of Albano. He was canonised on 14 April 1482 by Pope Sixtus IV. In 1588 Pope Sixtus V declared him a Doctor of the Church named as the "Seraphic Doctor" (Latin: Doctor Seraphicus). His feast day is 15 July.
Many writings from the Middle Ages once attributed to him have been subsequently re-classified under the name "Pseudo-Bonaventure".


Life
He was born at Civita di Bagnoregio, not far from Viterbo, then part of the Papal States. Almost nothing is known of his childhood, other than the names of his parents, Giovanni di Fidanza and Maria di Ritella. Bonaventure reports that in his youth he was saved from an untimely death by the prayers of Francis of Assisi, which is the primary motivation for Bonaventure's writing the vita.
He entered the Franciscan Order in 1243 and studied at the University of Paris, possibly under Alexander of Hales, and certainly under Alexander's successor, John of Rochelle. In 1253 he held the Franciscan chair at Paris. A dispute between seculars and mendicants delayed his reception as Master until 1257, where his degree was taken in friendship with Thomas Aquinas. Bonaventure also met and was a friend of the cardinal Hugh of Saint-Cher, by whom he was influenced.
Three years earlier his fame had earned him the position of lecturer on The Four Books of Sentences—a book of theology written by Peter Lombard in the twelfth century—and in 1255 he received the degree of master, the medieval equivalent of doctor.
After having successfully defended his order against the reproaches of the anti-mendicant party, he was elected Minister General of the Franciscan Order. On 24 November 1265, he was selected for the post of Archbishop of York; however, he was never consecrated and resigned the appointment in October 1266.
During his tenure, the General Chapter of Narbonne, held in 1260, promulgated a decree prohibiting the publication of any work out of the order without permission from superiors. This prohibition has induced modern writers to pass severe judgment upon Roger Bacon's superiors, who were assumed to be envious of Bacon's abilities. However, the prohibition enjoined on Bacon was a general one, which extended to the whole order. Its promulgation was not directed against him, but rather against Gerard of Borgo San Donnino. In 1254 Gerard had published without permission a work, Introductorius in Evangelium æternum (An Introduction to the Eternal Gospel) that was judged heretical within a year. Thereupon the General Chapter of Narbonne promulgated their decree, identical with the "constitutio gravis in contrarium" Bacon speaks of. The prohibition was rescinded in Roger's favour unexpectedly in 1266.

Bonaventure was instrumental in procuring the election of Pope Gregory X, who rewarded him with the title of Cardinal Bishop of Albano, and insisted on his presence at the great Second Council of Lyon in 1274. There, after his significant contributions led to a union of the Greek and Latin churches, Bonaventure died suddenly and under suspicious circumstances. The 1913 edition of the Catholic Encyclopedia has citations that suggest he was poisoned, but no mention is made of this in the 2003 second edition of the New Catholic Encyclopedia.
He steered the Franciscans on a moderate and intellectual course that made them the most prominent order in the Catholic Church until the coming of the Jesuits. His theology was marked by an attempt completely to integrate faith and reason. He thought of Christ as the "one true master" who offers humans knowledge that begins in faith, is developed through rational understanding, and is perfected by mystical union with God.

grok_lead: Saint Bonaventure (1221â1274), born Giovanni di Fidanza in Bagnoregio, Italy, was a prominent Italian Catholic Franciscan friar, theologian, philosopher, and prelate who served as Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor and later as Cardinal-Bishop of Albano. Known as the Seraphic Doctor for his profound mystical writings and integration of theology with spirituality, he is recognized as a Doctor of the Church and is often credited as the "second founder" of the Franciscan Order due to his efforts in organizing and revitalizing it amid internal conflicts. His life exemplified a harmonious blend of intellectual rigor and devotion, influencing medieval Christian thought through works that emphasized the soul's ascent to God via divine illumination and contemplation. Bonaventure joined the Franciscan Order around 1243, shortly after a childhood illness from which he was reportedly cured through the intercession of Saint Francis of Assisi, an event that inspired his lifelong commitment to the order. He pursued advanced studies at the University of Paris under the theologian Alexander of Hales, earning the title of master in 1253 and producing significant commentaries on Peter Lombard's Sentences, which became foundational texts in scholastic theology. During this period, Bonaventure also defended the mendicant orders against university opposition, establishing himself as a defender of Franciscan ideals of poverty and simplicity. Elected Minister General of the Friars Minor on February 2, 1257, Bonaventure led the order for seventeen years, implementing reforms such as the Constitutiones Narbonenses in 1260 to standardize governance and resolve disputes over the interpretation of Franciscan poverty. He authored the official biography of Saint Francis, the Legenda Major, which was approved by the order in 1263 and shaped Franciscan hagiography. Appointed Cardinal-Bishop of Albano by Pope Gregory X on June 23, 1273, he participated in the Second Council of Lyon, where he contributed to efforts for Church unity until his death on July 15, 1274, possibly from poisoning. Bonaventure's theological and philosophical contributions drew heavily on Neo-Platonism, integrating Platonic and Augustinian ideas with Aristotelian elements to argue for knowledge through divine illumination, where the soul ascends to God via reason, faith, and mystical union. Key works include the Itinerarium Mentis in Deum (1259), a mystical guide to the soul's journey toward divine ecstasy; the Breviloquium (1257), a comprehensive summary of sacred theology; and De Reductione Artium ad Theologiam, which subordinates all sciences to theology as paths to understanding God. His emphasis on the harmony of creation, exemplified in cosmological arguments for God's existence, and his revision of eudaimonism through Christian virtues profoundly influenced medieval mysticism and scholasticism. Canonized in 1482 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1588, Bonaventure's legacy endures in Franciscan spirituality, Catholic doctrine, and philosophical traditions that prioritize experiential knowledge of the divine over mere rationalism. His writings continue to inspire theologians and mystics, underscoring the unity of heart and mind in the pursuit of holiness.
